abstract:
Rapid advances in cowork agents are shifting human-AI collaboration toward real-world automation, delivering software, designs, and other artifacts. However, such productivity work demands both high-quality delivery on complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring and decision-making over long horizons, a combination that remains an open challenge. We introduce CoworkOS, a general-purpose harness for long-horizon work that separates task strategy from execution management: the model decides actions, delegation, and acceptance, while the runtime maintains state and feedback. Its three-layer architecture enables direct execution or delegation to Subagents, synchronously or asynchronously, under stable responsibilities. Through a shared application layer, humans and agents inspect and revise the same evolving documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes, so human-in-the-loop participation can enter both through conversation and through direct modification of the work itself. To sustain continuity across agents and sessions, CoworkOS further introduces hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory, so working files, key decisions, and long-running Job logs remain shareable, reusable, and resumable after interruption. Across 12 benchmarks and 6 categories of real-world applications, CoworkOS proves highly competitive with frontier agent applications such as Codex and DeepSeek Harness. As a sustained-work case study, CoworkOS uses GLM-5.3 as its backbone to conduct RSI-driven automated post-training on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Over five rounds, the model’s average score across eight benchmarks rose from 33.19 to 42.95 (+9.76). Looking ahead, we believe CoworkOS opens a meaningful path toward general cowork-agent intelligence.

Repo Link: github.com/RUC-NLPIR/CoworkOS

sections.body: The paper asks whether one cowork agent can carry complex productivity tasks and continued monitoring while humans stay in the loop. CoworkOS has three layers: a Main Agent that decides actions, delegation, and acceptance; a Coordinator Runtime that maintains state, feedback, and delegated work; and optional Subagents with separate contexts. Humans and agents inspect and revise the same documents, presentations, CAD models, and Blender scenes. Hierarchical workspaces and persistent semantic memory keep files, decisions, and Job logs resumable after interruption. The introduction also reports a post-training case study in which the average score moves from 33.19 to 42.95.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: CoworkOS splits task strategy from execution so one agent can handle complex delivery and long-horizon monitoring.

sections.body: This section formalizes an agent task as a tuple of objective, environment, action space, acceptance criterion, and resource budget. State evolves through agent actions, human edits, and external changes, and the objective is to maximize the probability of acceptance within budget. Agency is described along two dimensions: task complexity, meaning the number and interdependence of decisions, and temporal extent, meaning how long the objective stays active. Complex delivery mainly challenges the first dimension, while monitoring mainly challenges the second. Recursive self-improvement is presented as their intersection. The section gives a framing only and reports no experimental results.
sections.heading: Preliminaries: Task Formulation and Agency
sections.headline: Agent tasks are defined by objective, environment, actions, acceptance, and budget, judged along complexity and temporal extent.

sections.body: Main owns task-level decisions and can act directly, request human input, or delegate scoped work. A delegation specifies the objective, constraints, granted capabilities, and expected evidence. Synchronous calls keep results on Main's path, while asynchronous calls return an identifier and deliver results to Main's Inbox at a later decision boundary. Each Subagent runs in a separate context and returns a report, evidence references, and execution status. The Coordinator Runtime stores assignments, leases, and acknowledgements in persistent state so delivery survives interruption. Subagents can message peers asynchronously, but Main keeps task scope and final acceptance. The section describes design only and reports no experiments.
sections.heading: The CoworkOS Agent Harness
sections.headline: A three-layer harness with synchronous or asynchronous delegation, shared application objects, and durable workspaces and memory.

sections.body: The benchmark study covers 12 benchmarks in four domains: Tool Use, Productivity, Search, and ML Coding. GLM-5.3 runs with High thinking effort, a 256K-token context window, and a maximum output of 64K tokens per response. CoworkOS is compared with OpenHands, Codex, and DeepSeek Harness. Its Tool Use average is 55.22 against 55.31 for DeepSeek Harness, its Productivity average is 57.54 against 56.13, its Search average is 82.14 against 82.22 for OpenHands, and its ML Coding average is 56.26 against 56.14. Qualitative comparisons cover 24 real-world cases, judged from inspected deliverables rather than ranked. The text states that these observations are case-dependent and do not establish that CoworkOS leads on every scene detail.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: CoworkOS ranks among the top two harnesses in every domain average, leading Productivity and ML Coding.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the central design: Main selects and coordinates the work, while the runtime manages delegated execution, communication, shared application resources, persistent workspaces, semantic memory, and Jobs. Across 12 benchmarks and six categories of application cases, CoworkOS is described as competitive with OpenHands, Codex, and DeepSeek Harness. In the post-training study, the average score of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B rises from 33.19 to 42.95 over five rounds and eight benchmarks. The authors state that the gains vary across tasks. They conclude that the results support a unified harness for complex productivity work, continued monitoring, and iterative model improvement.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Post-training gains vary across tasks, and the paper concludes that one harness supports productivity, monitoring, and model improvement.

sections.body: The appendix gives benchmark-specific settings for all twelve benchmarks, including task counts, timeouts, retrieval setup, and graders. It describes the Elo calculation and tie-adjusted win rate used for GDPVal, and the equal weighting used for domain averages. The case evidence section gives inspection protocols for 24 cases and 72 artifacts and records limits such as the absence of calibrated lighting. The post-training records describe BM25 task-similarity filtering with a threshold of 0.8 and training-history deduplication. Table 2 reports all eight benchmark scores for R0 through R5, and the training lineage lists the five seed sources for R0.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists benchmark settings, scoring rules, case inspection protocols, and post-training run records with complete round scores.
